reels.title: How the Fed moves the whole market
reels.summary: The Federal Reserve sets short-term interest rates. Those rates ripple into mortgages, corporate borrowing, the dollar and stock valuations.

scenes.headline: One meeting can move **every** asset on Earth.
scenes.body: Here's how the Federal Reserve does it, in 60 seconds.

scenes.headline: The Fed's two jobs
scenes.body: Congress gave the Fed a **dual mandate**: maximum employment and stable prices. It aims for about **2% inflation** over time.

scenes.headline: Its main lever: the fed funds rate
items: The FOMC meets **8 times a year** to set a target for overnight bank lending rates
Raise rates → borrowing gets pricier → spending and inflation cool
Cut rates → money gets cheaper → growth (and risk-taking) picks up

scenes.headline: Why stocks care
scenes.body:
A stock is worth its future profits, **discounted** back to today. Higher rates shrink what those future dollars are worth, which hits fast-growing tech stocks hardest.

That's why markets hang on every word from the Fed Chair.

scenes.text: Higher interest rates shrink the value of ___ profits, which hits growth stocks hardest.

scenes.question: If the Fed unexpectedly raises rates, what usually happens to long-duration growth stocks?
scenes.explain: Higher rates reduce the present value of profits far in the future, and growth stocks earn most of theirs far in the future.

reels.title: CPI: the inflation report Wall Street fears
reels.summary: The Consumer Price Index measures how fast prices rise. Hot readings raise the odds of higher rates.

scenes.headline: Why one number at 8:30 a.m. can tank the market
scenes.body: Meet CPI, the Consumer Price Index.

scenes.headline: What CPI measures
scenes.body: Each month the **Bureau of Labor Statistics** prices a basket of goods and services that households buy: rent, food, gas, cars, haircuts, and more.

scenes.headline: Headline vs. core
items: **Headline CPI** includes everything
**Core CPI** strips out food and energy, which swing wildly
Markets usually focus on core, since it shows the underlying trend
The Fed's favorite gauge is a cousin: **PCE** inflation

scenes.headline: The market reaction
scenes.body: What moves stocks is the **surprise** versus forecasts, not the number itself. A hotter-than-expected print can push yields up and stocks down in minutes.

scenes.text: Markets react to the ___ versus forecasts, not the inflation number itself.

scenes.question: Which CPI measure removes food and energy prices?
scenes.explain: Core CPI excludes volatile food and energy, so it shows the stickier underlying trend.

reels.title: The yield curve, explained
reels.summary: The yield curve plots Treasury yields across maturities. When short rates exceed long rates (an inversion), it has often signaled a slowdown ahead.

scenes.headline: The recession signal economists watch most
scenes.body: It's called the yield curve. Here's how to read it.

scenes.headline: A normal curve slopes **up**
scenes.body: Illustrative. Lenders normally demand more interest to lock money up for longer.

scenes.headline: An inverted curve slopes **down**
scenes.body: Illustrative. Short rates are high (a tight Fed) while long rates are lower, because investors expect rate cuts and slower growth later.

scenes.headline: Signal, not a guarantee
scenes.body: Inversions have come before most US recessions since the 1960s. But the long 2022–2024 inversion was a reminder that timing is unreliable and false alarms happen.

scenes.text: When short-term yields are above long-term yields, the curve is ___.

scenes.question: An 'inverted' yield curve means…
options: Long-term yields are above short-term yields
Short-term yields are above long-term yields
scenes.explain: Inversion means short rates exceed long rates, the opposite of the normal upward slope.

sources.title: US Treasury: daily yield curve rates

reels.title: Why bond prices fall when yields rise
reels.summary: Existing bonds pay a fixed coupon. When new bonds pay more, old ones must get cheaper to compete.

scenes.headline: Bonds have a seesaw built in
scenes.body: When yields go up, prices go down. Here's why.

scenes.headline: Picture this
scenes.body: You own a 10-year bond paying **4%**. Next week, new bonds start paying **6%**. Nobody will pay full price for your 4% bond anymore, so its price drops until its total return matches 6%.

scenes.headline: Price of a 10-year, 4% bond
scenes.label: Market yield 2% → 7%
scenes.note: At a 2% yield it's worth **$118**. At 4% it's worth exactly $100. At 7% it falls to **$79**.

scenes.headline: Why stock traders care
scenes.body: The 10-year Treasury yield is the market's "risk-free rate." When it jumps, stocks must offer more return to compete, so prices often fall. **Watch the 10-year.**

scenes.text: When market yields rise, existing bond prices ___.

scenes.question: A bond pays a 3% coupon. Market yields rise to 5%. Its price will…
scenes.explain: Its fixed 3% coupon is now less attractive than new 5% bonds, so its price must fall to compensate buyers.

reels.title: The P/E ratio in 60 seconds
reels.summary: Price-to-earnings tells you how many dollars investors pay for each dollar of a company's annual profit.

scenes.headline: Is a $500 stock expensive?
scenes.body: You can't tell from the price alone. You need the **P/E ratio**.

scenes.headline: Price ÷ Earnings per share
scenes.caption: $100 share price ÷ $4 of yearly profit per share

scenes.headline: How to read it
items: High P/E = investors expect fast growth (or it's overhyped)
Low P/E = slow growth, high risk, or a bargain
Compare within the same industry, since banks and software differ a lot
**Forward P/E** uses next year's expected earnings

scenes.headline: The catch
scenes.body: P/E breaks when earnings are tiny or negative. For young, unprofitable companies investors use price-to-sales or other measures instead.

scenes.text: P/E tells you how many dollars investors pay for each $1 of ___.

scenes.question: Stock A trades at $60 with $3 EPS. What's its P/E?
scenes.explain: $60 ÷ $3 = 20. Investors pay $20 for each $1 of annual profit.

reels.title: Earnings season: beats, misses & guidance
reels.summary: Four times a year companies report results. The stock reacts to results versus expectations, and above all to guidance.

scenes.headline: Why a stock can **drop** after a great quarter
scenes.body: Earnings season, decoded.

scenes.headline: What gets reported
items: **Revenue**: total sales
**EPS**: profit per share
**Margins**: how much of each sale becomes profit
**Guidance**: what management expects next

scenes.headline: It's all about expectations
scenes.body: Analysts publish estimates beforehand. Beating them is good, but if the market quietly expected a **bigger** beat (the "whisper number"), the stock can still fall.

scenes.headline: Guidance is king
scenes.body: Stocks are priced on the future. A company that beats this quarter but **lowers its outlook** often sells off hard, while a miss with raised guidance can rally.

scenes.text: Because stocks are priced on the future, ___ often matters more than last quarter's results.

scenes.question: A company beats EPS estimates but cuts next quarter's guidance. The stock most likely…
scenes.explain: Markets look forward. Weaker guidance lowers expected future profits, which usually outweighs a past beat.

reels.title: What the S&P 500 really is
reels.summary: The S&P 500 tracks about 500 large US companies, weighted by market value, so the biggest names dominate.

scenes.headline: "The market was up today." Which market?
scenes.body: Usually, the **S&P 500**.

scenes.headline: 500 of America's largest companies
scenes.body: A committee picks large, profitable US firms across all sectors. It's the most-used benchmark for US stocks.

scenes.headline: Weighted by size
scenes.body: It's **market-cap weighted**: a $3 trillion company moves the index far more than a $30 billion one. Lately the top 10 stocks make up **more than a third** of the whole index.

scenes.headline: Know the big three
items: **S&P 500**: broad large-cap benchmark
**Nasdaq Composite**: tech-heavy, growth-focused
**Dow Jones**: just 30 blue chips, weighted by share *price* (an old quirk)

scenes.text: The S&P 500 is weighted by ___, so the biggest companies move it most.

scenes.question: Why can a handful of tech stocks drive most of the S&P 500's move?
scenes.explain: Bigger companies get bigger weights, so a few giants can dominate daily moves.

reels.title: The VIX: Wall Street's fear gauge
reels.summary: The VIX uses options prices to estimate how much traders expect the S&P 500 to swing over the next 30 days.

scenes.headline: There's an index for **fear**
scenes.body: It's called the VIX.

scenes.headline: How it works
scenes.body: When traders rush to buy protection (put options), option prices rise. The VIX turns those prices into **expected volatility** for the next 30 days.

scenes.headline: Read it backwards
scenes.body: The VIX usually **rises when stocks fall**. Spikes often happen near market bottoms, when fear peaks. Contrarians sometimes call it a signal to get greedy.

scenes.text: The VIX usually ___ when stocks fall.

scenes.question: The S&P 500 drops sharply. The VIX usually…
scenes.explain: Falling stocks drive demand for protection, which pushes option prices and the VIX higher.

reels.title: The US dollar and your stocks
reels.summary: A strong dollar makes US exports pricier and shrinks foreign profits when converted back, which matters for multinationals.

scenes.headline: A strong dollar isn't always good news
scenes.body: Here's how currencies hit stock prices.

scenes.headline: Meet the DXY
scenes.body: The **US Dollar Index** measures the dollar against six major currencies, mostly the euro, plus the yen, pound and others.

scenes.headline: When the dollar rises…
items: US companies' **foreign sales** convert back into fewer dollars
US exports get pricier abroad
Emerging markets with dollar debt feel squeezed
Commodities priced in dollars (like oil and gold) often dip

scenes.headline: Who wins?
scenes.body: Importers and US travelers abroad. And when the dollar **weakens**, big multinationals like Apple or Coca-Cola often get a boost to reported earnings.

scenes.text: A stronger dollar shrinks the ___ profits of US multinationals.

scenes.question: A sharply stronger dollar tends to hurt which companies most?
options: US multinationals with big overseas sales
scenes.explain: Overseas revenue converts back into fewer dollars, so reported earnings shrink.

reels.title: How oil prices ripple through the economy
reels.summary: Oil feeds into transport, manufacturing and consumer budgets. Spikes act like a tax on consumers and can lift inflation.

scenes.headline: A barrel of oil touches almost everything
scenes.body: From your gas tank to grocery prices.

scenes.headline: When oil spikes
items: [up]Energy stocks[/up] usually rise
[down]Airlines, truckers, cruise lines[/down] get squeezed
Consumers spend more on gas and less elsewhere
Inflation ticks up, so the Fed stays cautious

scenes.headline: Who sets the price?
scenes.body: Global supply and demand: **OPEC+** output decisions, US shale production, Chinese demand, and geopolitical risk in places like the Middle East and Russia.

scenes.headline: Two benchmarks
scenes.body: **WTI** (US crude, priced in Cushing, Oklahoma) and **Brent** (the North Sea global benchmark). They usually move together.

scenes.text: Higher oil prices help ___ but hurt airlines and truckers.

scenes.question: Oil jumps 20% on a supply shock. Which sector is most likely to benefit?
scenes.explain: Producers sell their oil at higher prices; transport companies pay more for fuel.

sources.title: EIA: What drives crude oil prices

reels.title: The jobs report: the first Friday ritual
reels.summary: The monthly Employment Situation report shows payroll growth, unemployment and wages, which are key inputs for the Fed.

scenes.headline: First Friday of the month, 8:30 a.m. ET
scenes.body: The jobs report drops, and markets move.

scenes.headline: What's inside
items: **Nonfarm payrolls**: jobs added or lost
**Unemployment rate**: share of the labor force looking for work
**Average hourly earnings**: wage growth, a clue to inflation

scenes.headline: Good news can be bad news
scenes.body: A blowout jobs number shows a strong economy. But it can also mean the Fed keeps rates **higher for longer**, so stocks sometimes fall on "good" news.

scenes.headline: Watch the revisions
scenes.body: Prior months get revised as more data arrives. Big downward revisions can matter as much as the headline.

scenes.text: A very hot jobs report can hurt stocks if it keeps the Fed's rates ___.

scenes.question: Why might stocks fall on a much stronger-than-expected jobs report?
options: It may mean the Fed keeps rates high
scenes.explain: A hot labor market can keep inflation pressure up, delaying rate cuts that markets were hoping for.

reels.title: GDP & recessions, explained
reels.summary: GDP measures the total output of the economy. Recessions are broad, lasting declines in activity, officially dated by the NBER.

scenes.headline: What actually counts as a recession?
scenes.body: It's not as simple as you've heard.

scenes.headline: GDP = the economy's scoreboard
scenes.body: Gross Domestic Product is the value of everything produced in the US. It's reported **quarterly** and annualized. About **two-thirds** is consumer spending.

scenes.headline: The rule of thumb
scenes.body: Two straight quarters of shrinking GDP is a popular shorthand for a recession, but it's **not** the official definition.

scenes.headline: The official call
scenes.body: In the US, a committee at the **National Bureau of Economic Research** declares recessions by looking at jobs, income, spending and production, often months after the fact.

scenes.text: About two-thirds of US GDP comes from ___ spending.

scenes.question: Who officially dates US recessions?
scenes.explain: The National Bureau of Economic Research's Business Cycle Dating Committee makes the call.

reels.title: Cyclical vs. defensive stocks
reels.summary: Some sectors boom and bust with the economy; others hold up because people buy their products no matter what.

scenes.headline: Why some stocks hold up in a recession
scenes.body: Cyclical vs. defensive, in one minute.

scenes.headline: Cyclical: ride the economy
items: Consumer discretionary (cars, travel, retail)
Industrials & materials
Financials
Energy

scenes.headline: Defensive: steady demand
items: Consumer staples (food, toothpaste)
Utilities
Healthcare

scenes.headline: Sector rotation
scenes.body: Investors shift money between these groups as they change their view of the economy. When defensives lead while the market falls, it's often a **risk-off** signal.

scenes.text: Utilities, staples and healthcare are ___ sectors that hold up in downturns.

scenes.question: Which sector is typically considered defensive?
scenes.explain: People pay electric and water bills in good times and bad, so utilities' earnings are steadier.

reels.title: Compounding: the 8th wonder
reels.summary: Returns that earn their own returns grow exponentially. Time in the market is the biggest lever.

scenes.headline: $10,000. 7% a year. Do nothing.
scenes.body: What happens after 30 years?

scenes.headline: Growth of $10,000 at 7%/yr
scenes.label: Years 0 → 30
scenes.note: It's about **$19,672** after 10 years and **$38,697** after 20, then the curve bends sharply upward.

scenes.headline: The Rule of 72
scenes.body: Divide 72 by your annual return to estimate years to double. At 7%, money doubles roughly every **10 years**. At 10%, every **7**.

scenes.headline: The lesson
scenes.body: Starting early matters more than picking the perfect stock. Fees and taxes compound too, **against** you.

scenes.text: By the Rule of 72, money earning 7% a year doubles about every ___ years.

scenes.question: Using the Rule of 72, how long does money take to double at 9% a year?
scenes.explain: 72 ÷ 9 = 8 years.

reels.title: Index funds & ETFs
reels.summary: ETFs let you buy a whole basket of stocks in one trade, cheaply and with instant diversification.

scenes.headline: Own 500 companies with one click
scenes.body: That's what an index ETF does.

scenes.headline: What's an ETF?
scenes.body: An **exchange-traded fund** holds a basket of assets and trades like a single stock. An S&P 500 ETF owns every company in the index.

scenes.headline: Why investors love them
items: Instant diversification: one bad stock can't sink you
Very low fees (some under 0.05% a year)
Trade any time the market is open

scenes.headline: The tough truth
scenes.body: Over long periods, most actively managed funds **trail** their index benchmark after fees. That's the case for passive investing.

scenes.text: An index ETF gives you instant ___ at a very low cost.

scenes.question: The main benefit of a broad index ETF is…
scenes.explain: You spread risk across many companies for a small fee, but you still ride market ups and downs.

reels.title: Dividends vs. buybacks
reels.summary: Two ways companies return cash to shareholders: paying it out directly, or shrinking the share count.

scenes.headline: A company made a profit. Now what?
scenes.body: Two ways to hand the cash back to you.

scenes.headline: Dividends
scenes.body: Cash paid directly to shareholders, usually **quarterly**. The **dividend yield** = annual dividend ÷ share price. A $100 stock paying $3 a year yields 3%.

scenes.headline: Buybacks
scenes.body: The company buys its own shares and retires them. Fewer shares means each remaining share owns a bigger slice, so **EPS rises** even if profit doesn't.

scenes.headline: Watch out for
items: Very high yields can signal a dividend cut is coming
Buybacks at sky-high prices can destroy value
Borrowing to fund either one can weaken the balance sheet

scenes.text: Buybacks reduce the share count, which raises ___ per share.

scenes.question: A $50 stock pays $2 per year in dividends. Its yield is…

reels.title: Free cash flow: the number pros trust
reels.summary: Free cash flow is the cash a business generates after paying to maintain and grow its assets. It's harder to fudge than earnings.

scenes.headline: Profits are an opinion. Cash is a fact.
scenes.body: Meet free cash flow.

scenes.headline: The formula
scenes.caption: Operating cash flow minus capital expenditures

scenes.headline: Why it matters
scenes.body: Accounting earnings involve judgment calls. FCF is the actual cash left over, which pays dividends, buybacks, acquisitions and debt.

scenes.headline: FCF yield
scenes.body: FCF ÷ market cap. A 5% FCF yield means the business generates cash equal to 5% of its price each year, a handy way to compare valuations.

scenes.text: Free cash flow = operating cash flow minus ___.

scenes.question: A company has $10B operating cash flow and $4B capex. Its free cash flow is…
scenes.explain: $10B − $4B = $6B of free cash flow.

reels.title: Economic moats: why great companies stay great
reels.summary: A moat is a durable competitive advantage that protects profits from competitors.

scenes.headline: Warren Buffett's favorite word: **moat**
scenes.body: What makes a business hard to beat?

scenes.headline: The 5 classic moats
items: **Network effects**: more users make it more valuable (Visa, marketplaces)
**Switching costs**: painful to leave (enterprise software)
**Brand / intangibles**: patents, licenses, loyalty
**Cost advantage**: cheapest producer at scale (Costco)
**Efficient scale**: niche markets that only support a few players

scenes.headline: Why it matters for stocks
scenes.body: Wide-moat companies can keep high returns on capital for decades. That's why investors often pay premium valuations for them.

scenes.text: A durable competitive advantage that protects profits is called a ___.

scenes.question: A business software tool that's painful for customers to replace has which moat?
scenes.explain: Retraining staff and migrating data makes customers reluctant to leave.

reels.title: Risk-on vs. risk-off
reels.summary: Markets swing between appetite for risk and a rush to safety. Spotting which mode you're in explains a lot of daily moves.

scenes.headline: Why does everything move together some days?
scenes.body: Markets have two moods.

scenes.headline: Risk-on 🟢
items: Stocks up, especially tech and small caps
High-yield bonds and crypto rally
VIX falls

scenes.headline: Risk-off 🔴
items: Stocks fall, defensives outperform
Treasuries, gold, yen and the dollar often rise
VIX spikes

scenes.headline: Use it
scenes.body: When stocks drop, check the rest: if bonds and gold rally and the VIX jumps, it's a broad flight to safety, not just one company's bad news.

scenes.text: On risk-off days, investors flee to safe havens like ___.

scenes.question: Which asset tends to rise on a risk-off day?
scenes.explain: Investors flee to safe havens like Treasuries, pushing their prices up and yields down.

reels.title: Short selling & short squeezes
reels.summary: Shorting is betting a stock will fall. When shorts rush to cover, prices can spike violently.

scenes.headline: How do you profit when a stock **falls**?
scenes.body: You short it. Here's how that works and how it backfires.

scenes.headline: Short selling, step by step
items: Borrow shares from a broker and sell them at $100
Wait for the price to drop to $70
Buy them back and return them, keeping $30

scenes.headline: The danger
scenes.body: A stock can only fall to $0, but it can rise **without limit**. Short sellers face theoretically unlimited losses.

scenes.headline: The squeeze
scenes.body: If a heavily shorted stock jumps, shorts scramble to buy back shares, which pushes the price even higher. GameStop in January 2021 is the famous example.

scenes.text: A short seller profits when the stock price ___.

scenes.question: What's the maximum loss on a short position?
scenes.explain: There's no ceiling on how high a stock can rise, so losses on a short have no hard limit.

reels.title: Share price vs. market cap
reels.summary: A high share price doesn't make a company big. Market cap, price times shares outstanding, does.

scenes.headline: Is a $900 stock 'bigger' than a $90 one?
scenes.body: Not necessarily.

scenes.headline: Market cap
scenes.caption: The total value the market puts on a company

scenes.headline: Example
scenes.body: Company B is **5× bigger** despite a share price one-tenth as high.

scenes.headline: Stock splits change nothing
scenes.body: A 10-for-1 split turns one $900 share into ten $90 shares. The company's value is identical; it just looks cheaper.

scenes.text: Market cap = share price × ___.

scenes.question: After a 4-for-1 stock split, a company's market cap…
scenes.explain: There are 4× the shares at ¼ the price, so the total value is unchanged.

reels.title: Corrections, bear markets & bull markets
reels.summary: Market drawdowns have names based on how far prices fall from a recent peak.

scenes.headline: Stocks are down 12%. Is it a crash?
scenes.body: Here's the official lingo.

scenes.headline: And a bull market?
scenes.body: A rise of **20% or more** from a recent low. Historically, bull markets have lasted much longer than bear markets.

scenes.headline: Perspective
scenes.body: Corrections are normal; the S&P 500 has seen one every year or two on average. Selling in a panic often locks in losses right before recoveries.

scenes.text: A drop of 20% or more from a peak is called a ___ market.

scenes.question: The S&P 500 falls 22% from its high. That's a…
scenes.explain: A decline of 20% or more from a peak is the common definition of a bear market.

reels.title: How to read a candlestick
reels.summary: Each candle shows four prices for a period: open, high, low and close.

scenes.headline: Those red and green bars? They're candlesticks.
scenes.body: Each one tells a story about a trading day.

scenes.headline: Anatomy of a candle
items: **Body**: the range between open and close
**Green** = closed higher than it opened; **red** = closed lower
**Wicks**: the day's high and low

scenes.headline: Reading the wicks
scenes.body: A long lower wick means sellers pushed the price down but buyers fought it back, a possible sign of support. A long upper wick shows rejection at higher prices.

scenes.headline: Keep it in context
scenes.body: Candle patterns are clues, not crystal balls. Volume and the bigger trend matter more than any single candle.

scenes.text: A green candle means the price closed ___ than it opened.

scenes.question: A green candle means the price…
scenes.explain: Green (or hollow) candles close higher than they opened for that period.

reels.title: Tariffs & trade wars, explained
reels.summary: Tariffs are taxes on imports. They can protect domestic industries but raise costs and invite retaliation.

scenes.headline: Who actually pays a tariff?
scenes.body: Spoiler: usually not the foreign country.

scenes.headline: What it is
scenes.body: A tariff is a **tax on imported goods**, paid by the importing company when goods cross the border. Costs are often passed on to customers.

scenes.headline: Market effects
items: Companies with global supply chains face higher costs and margin pressure
Some domestic producers gain pricing power
Retaliation can hit exporters (farm goods, chips, aircraft)
Uncertainty itself can weigh on business investment

scenes.headline: What to watch
scenes.body: Which countries and products are targeted, exemptions, and how companies talk about tariff costs on earnings calls.

scenes.text: A tariff is a tax on ___ goods.

scenes.question: A US tariff on imported steel is paid directly by…
options: The US company importing the steel
scenes.explain: The importer pays the duty at the border, then often passes some of the cost on.

reels.title: Dollar-cost averaging
reels.summary: Investing a fixed amount on a schedule buys more shares when prices are low and fewer when high.

scenes.headline: Don't know when to buy? Don't pick.
scenes.body: Dollar-cost averaging takes timing off the table.

scenes.headline: $100 a month into a bumpy stock
scenes.label: Price over 10 months
scenes.note: $1,000 invested buys **21.8 shares**, an average cost of **$45.90**, below the $47.00 average price, because you bought more shares when it was cheap.

scenes.headline: Why it works for humans
scenes.body: It removes the urge to time the market and turns dips into automatic bargains. It's how most people invest through workplace retirement plans.

scenes.text: Dollar-cost averaging buys ___ shares when prices are low.

scenes.question: With dollar-cost averaging, when the price drops you…
options: Buy more shares with the same dollars
scenes.explain: A fixed dollar amount buys more shares at lower prices.
